passages.title: Owen Blake on a coastal fishery (1970)
passages.body: Owen Blake's 1970 essay on a coastal fishery opens with a scene that looks minor: a form, a caption, a roster. The argument is that politeness can be a method of exclusion. The writer notes that nostalgia for a slower era is itself a politics. The turn is that the complaint is not against method but against unacknowledged method. Examples accumulate without becoming a catalogue — a mistranslated notice, a map that omits a creek, a hiring rubric that scores “fit.” The prose is dry rather than outraged; the heat is in what is treated as obvious. A late paragraph asks what would have to be true for the current procedure to be called fair, and then shows that those conditions are not met. The essay does not offer a slogan. It offers a test: if a practice cannot survive being described without its official adjectives, the adjectives were doing the work. Readers who want a policy list will be disappointed; readers who want to see how a tone becomes a rule will not. Seed 0 only changes the proper names and the arena; the argumentative shape stays this concession-then-turn.

questions.explanation: Main idea tracks the turn after the concession: standards exist, but they are being used to hide a choice about speakers in a coastal fishery. Biography, a universal policy list, and anti-standard populism are the usual CARS overreads. The proper names (Owen Blake, seed 0) are cover, not the purpose.

distractor_rationales.A: The passage is not a biography.
distractor_rationales.C: It does not reject standards; it says they hide a choice.
